The word passage has several distinct meanings, all connected by one underlying idea: something moves through or from one point to another — whether that's a person, a piece of writing, a law, or even time itself.
1. A physical path or narrow way through something

This is the most concrete meaning. A passage is a narrow route, corridor, or opening that allows you to move from one place to another. Think of it as a "through-way."

  • The dark, narrow passage between the two buildings led to the garden.
  • The underground passage connected the main hall to the kitchen.
  • A secret passage behind the bookshelf led to a hidden room.

The key idea here is narrowness and function — it exists specifically so that movement through it is possible. A wide-open field is not a passage. A hallway, a tunnel, an alleyway, a channel of water between two landmasses — these are passages.

In anatomy, the same idea applies to tunnels inside the body:

  • Your nasal passages are the channels inside your nose through which air travels.
  • The birth passage (also called the birth canal) is the channel through which a baby is born.
2. A section taken from a piece of writing or music

When you pick out a portion of a book, article, speech, scripture, or musical composition, that portion is called a passage. It is not the whole work — just a selected part of it, usually meaningful on its own.

  • The teacher asked the students to read the passage on page 47 carefully.
  • He recited a beautiful passage from the Quran.
  • The opening passage of the novel immediately drew me in.
  • The pianist played a difficult passage from Beethoven's sonata.

Think of it this way: just as a passage in a building takes you through a portion of it, a passage in a text takes you through a portion of the writer's thoughts.
3. The act of moving through, past, or across something

Passage can also refer to the act or process of passing through something — the movement itself, not just the route.

  • The army was denied passage through the mountain territory.
  • The ship's passage through the narrow strait was treacherous.
  • The whale's passage through the bay was watched by hundreds of people.

Here, passage means the journey, crossing, or movement — the fact that something went through or across a space.
4. A journey, especially by sea or air

Closely related to the above, passage is specifically used for a trip or voyage — most classically, a journey by ship across an ocean or sea.

  • They booked passage on a steamship to England.
  • The passage from Mumbai to London took several weeks by ship in those days.
  • He worked on the boat in exchange for free passage to the new world.

Notice that in this meaning, passage often replaces the word "trip" or "voyage." It carries a slightly old-fashioned, literary tone and is most naturally used with sea or air travel.

When time goes by — hours, days, years — we call this the passage of time. You cannot stop it; it moves forward continuously.

  • With the passage of time, her grief slowly faded.
  • The passage of decades changed the city beyond recognition.
  • The poem is about the passage of seasons from youth to old age.

This is a figurative extension of the core idea: time, too, "moves through" from one point to another.
6. A transition from one stage or state of life to another

A passage can refer to a significant change or move from one phase of life, status, or condition to a new one. This is closely linked to the phrase rite of passage — a ceremony or experience that marks a major life transition.

  • Marriage, graduation, and the birth of a child are all passages in a person's life.
  • His first solo journey abroad was a passage into adulthood.
  • A rite of passage is any ritual that marks a person's transition to a new role — for example, a coming-of-age ceremony.
7. The official approval of a law or bill

In politics and government, passage refers to the process of a proposed law (a "bill") being officially approved and accepted by a legislature or governing body.

  • The passage of the new education bill was celebrated widely.
  • After years of debate, the law finally achieved passage in parliament.
  • The senator fought hard for the passage of the climate reform act.

Again, the core idea holds: the bill "passes through" the legislative process and comes out the other side as law.
8. The right or permission to travel through a place

Sometimes passage refers not to the act of traveling, but to the right or permission to travel through a particular area or territory. It is most common in formal, legal, or diplomatic contexts.

  • The ship requested passage through the neutral country's waters.
  • They granted passage to refugees crossing the border.
  • He was given safe passage out of the country after the negotiations.

"Safe passage" is a very common phrase meaning a guarantee that someone will be allowed to travel without being harmed, stopped, or arrested.

Every meaning of passage comes back to the same core idea: movement through a space, a piece, a stage, or a process. Whether it is:

  • a corridor you walk through,
  • a section of a book you read through,
  • a journey you travel through,
  • time that passes through,
  • a stage of life you move through, or
  • a law that works its way through government —

in every case, something is going from one side to the other, from one point to the next. That is the soul of the word passage.
